## This afternoon

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | What a network **is** | from the logistic regression you own to a hidden layer |
| **2** | How it **learns** | loss → gradient descent → backpropagation, **worked by hand with real numbers** |
| **3** | How to keep it **honest** | capacity, weight decay, dropout, early stopping, scaling |
| **4** | How to **fit one in R** | `mlp()` + `nnet`; `brulee` + torch; tuning; SHAP |
| **5** | When it is the **wrong tool** | the evidence on tabular data |
| **6** | What **deep learning** adds | CNNs, RNNs, transformers; how they fail in health |

::: {.say}
By 16.40 you will have trained, tuned and explained a network with the same six verbs as every other model —
and you will know exactly which numbers changed when it "learned".
:::

## Seventy years in one slide

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 1958 | **Perceptron** (Rosenblatt) | one neuron; can only draw a line |
| 1969 | Minsky & Papert | "it can't do XOR" — first AI winter |
| 1986 | **Backpropagation** popularised (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams) | hidden layers become trainable |
| 1989–91 | Universal approximation (Cybenko; Hornik) | one wide hidden layer can fit any continuous function |
| 1998 | LeNet reads cheques (LeCun) | convolution works; compute and data are scarce |
| 2012 | **AlexNet** wins ImageNet by a mile | GPUs + big data + ReLU + dropout: "deep learning" |
| 2016 | Diabetic retinopathy at specialist level (Gulshan et al., JAMA) | medicine notices |
| 2017 | **Transformers** (Vaswani et al.) | sequences, text, then everything |
| 2020s | Foundation models, LLMs, multimodal medical models | the current wave |

For **tabular** health data the story is quieter: trees still win most contests. We will see why, and we will see
it in our own data.

# 1 · What a network is {.section-slide .center background-color="#0b2545" background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #0b2545 0%, #0f4c6e 55%, #13838f 100%)"}

## You already own a neural network

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../images/gen/logistic_neuron.png)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Logistic regression:

$$p = \sigma(w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_p x_p + b), \qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$$

A **neuron** (unit): weighted sum → bias → non-linear **activation**. $w$ = weights, $b$ = bias.

That is the whole building block. Everything else is wiring.

Its limit is geometric: $p \ge 0.5 \iff z \ge 0$, and $z = 0$ is a **straight line** (a hyperplane). One neuron
draws one straight boundary.
:::
::::

## Why one neuron is not enough

![](../images/gen/nn_boundary_evolution.png){fig-align="center" height="300"}

- **XOR** and the **two rings**: no $w_1, w_2, b$ separate them. Logistic regression scores 55 %.
- Minsky & Papert (1969) made this point and the field stalled for fifteen years.
- The fix was obvious and un-trainable until backpropagation: let several neurons each draw a soft line, then let
  one more neuron **combine** the lines.

## The multilayer perceptron

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](../images/gen/mlp_2_8_1.png)
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
One hidden layer of $H$ units, one output, one person $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^p$:

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{z}^{(1)} &= \mathbf{W}^{(1)\top}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{a}^{(1)} &= g(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}) \\
z^{(2)} &= \mathbf{W}^{(2)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)} \\
p &= \sigma(z^{(2)})
\end{aligned}$$

$\mathbf{W}^{(1)}$: $p\times H$; $\mathbf{W}^{(2)}$: $H$ numbers. For $n$ people, stack $\mathbf{x}$ as rows of
$\mathbf{X}$ and it is all matrix multiplication → GPUs → five lines of R.

**Parameters:** $pH + 2H + 1$. For us ($p\approx45$, $H=30$): **1,411**.
:::
::::

## "Deep" just means more of the same

$$\mathbf{a}^{(2)} = g\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(2)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}\right), \qquad
\mathbf{a}^{(3)} = g\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(3)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(2)} + \mathbf{b}^{(3)}\right), \ \dots$$

![](../images/gen/mlp_deep.png){fig-align="center" height="330"}

Each layer re-describes the previous one's output. Depth lets a network **compose** simple features into complex
ones with far fewer units than one very wide layer would need (edges → textures → parts → objects).

## A worked forward pass — keep these numbers

2 inputs → 2 tanh units → 1 sigmoid output. One person, $\mathbf{x} = (1.0,\ 0.5)$, truly a case ($y = 1$).

$$\mathbf{W}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & -0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathbf{b}^{(1)} = (0.1,\ 0.1),\quad \mathbf{W}^{(2)} = (0.7,\ -0.4),\quad b^{(2)} = 0.05$$

| Step | Computation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| hidden pre-activations | $1.0(0.5)+0.5(0.2)+0.1$; $\ 1.0(-0.3)+0.5(0.8)+0.1$ | $(0.70,\ 0.20)$ |
| hidden activations | $\tanh(0.70),\ \tanh(0.20)$ | $(0.6044,\ 0.1974)$ |
| output pre-activation | $0.7(0.6044)-0.4(0.1974)+0.05$ | $0.3941$ |
| prediction | $\sigma(0.3941)$ | $\mathbf{p = 0.5973}$ |

The network says 60 % for someone who is a case. It should say more. **Training is how it learns to.**

## Activation functions: the non-linearity is the point

![](../images/gen/activations.png){fig-align="center" height="270"}

| | Formula | Derivative | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| sigmoid | $1/(1+e^{-z})$ | $\sigma(1-\sigma)$ | binary output; `nnet` hidden units |
| tanh | — | $1-\tanh^2 z$ | zero-centred; our from-scratch net |
| **ReLU** | $\max(0,z)$ | 1 if $z>0$ else 0 | default hidden unit in deep nets |
| softmax | $e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$ | — | multi-class output |

**Without a non-linear $g$, layers collapse**: a product of matrices is a matrix → one linear model. The squash is
what lets eight neurons make a ring.

**Saturation**: where sigmoid/tanh are flat, the derivative ≈ 0, so earlier layers stop learning — the
*vanishing gradient*. ReLU's derivative is exactly 1 on the positive side; that is most of why 2012 happened.

# 2 · How it learns {.section-slide .center background-color="#0b2545" background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #0b2545 0%, #0f4c6e 55%, #13838f 100%)"}

## The loss: what "wrong" means

$$L = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\Big[y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\Big]$$

- **Binary cross-entropy** = the negative log-likelihood logistic regression maximises. Nothing new.
- Punishes confident wrong answers brutally: $p=0.99$ when $y=0$ costs 4.6; $p=0.6$ costs 0.9.
- Smooth → has a gradient everywhere. *Accuracy* has no useful gradient, so nothing is trained on it directly.
- Regression: MSE. Multi-class: categorical cross-entropy. Survival/ordinal/custom: write your own.

For the worked example: $L = -\log(0.5973) = 0.5154$.

## Gradient descent: walk downhill

![](../images/gen/gradient_descent_lr.png){fig-align="center" height="280"}

$$\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta} \qquad \text{for every weight and bias}$$

1. Start with small random weights. 2. Compute the loss and its **gradient** (direction of steepest increase).
3. Step **against** it, by the **learning rate** η. 4. Repeat for many **epochs**.

Same knob, same trade-off as XGBoost's `learn_rate` this morning.

## Batches, momentum, Adam

| Variant | Gradient from | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| batch GD | all $n$ rows | exact; slow for large $n$ (Tutorial 7 Part B; `nnet` via BFGS) |
| stochastic (SGD) | one row | noisy; the noise helps escape poor regions |
| **mini-batch** | 32–512 rows | the standard; 1 epoch = all batches once (`brulee`, `torch`, `keras`) |
| momentum | running average of past gradients | rolls through flat regions, damps zig-zag |
| **Adam / AdamW** | per-weight adaptive step + momentum | default optimiser in most of deep learning |
| L-BFGS | uses curvature | excellent for small nets; `nnet` and `brulee`'s default |

A **learning-rate schedule** (decay, cyclic) often matters more than which optimiser.

## Backpropagation is the chain rule — step 1: the output

We need $\partial L/\partial\theta$ for every weight. One backward sweep, reusing each layer's result.

**Output layer.** Sigmoid + cross-entropy gives a small miracle:
$$\delta^{(2)} \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}} = p - y$$
*How wrong, with a sign.* Example: $\delta^{(2)} = 0.5973 - 1 = \mathbf{-0.4027}$.

Then, since $z^{(2)} = \sum_h W^{(2)}_h a^{(1)}_h + b^{(2)}$:
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(2)}_h} = \delta^{(2)} a^{(1)}_h, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)}$$

Example: $\partial L/\partial\mathbf{W}^{(2)} = -0.4027\times(0.6044,\ 0.1974) = (-0.2434,\ -0.0795)$.

## Step 2: pass the blame back through the hidden layer

How much did each hidden activation contribute to the error?
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(1)}_h} = \delta^{(2)}\,W^{(2)}_h \;\Rightarrow\; (-0.4027)(0.7,\ -0.4) = (-0.2819,\ 0.1611)$$

Through the activation ($a = \tanh z$, so multiply by $1 - a^2$):
$$\delta^{(1)}_h = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(1)}_h}\,(1-(a^{(1)}_h)^2) \;\Rightarrow\; (-0.2819)(0.6347),\ (0.1611)(0.9610) = (-0.1789,\ 0.1548)$$

Input weights ($z^{(1)}_h = \sum_j W^{(1)}_{jh}x_j + b^{(1)}_h$):
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}_{jh}} = \delta^{(1)}_h\,x_j \;\Rightarrow\;
\begin{pmatrix}1.0\\0.5\end{pmatrix}(-0.1789,\ 0.1548) = \begin{pmatrix}-0.1789 & 0.1548\\ -0.0895 & 0.0774\end{pmatrix}$$

## Step 3: one gradient-descent step, η = 0.5

$$\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \to \begin{pmatrix}0.5895 & -0.3774\\ 0.2447 & 0.7613\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathbf{b}^{(1)} \to (0.1895,\ 0.0226),\quad
\mathbf{W}^{(2)} \to (0.8217,\ -0.3603),\quad b^{(2)} \to 0.2514$$

Forward pass again with the new weights: $\mathbf{p = 0.6966}$, loss $0.3615$ (was 0.5154).

::: {.key}
The network moved toward the right answer for this person. Average the gradients over all $n$ people, repeat a
few thousand times, and it has *learned*. **That is all learning means here: the numbers in $\mathbf{W}$ changed.**
:::

Frameworks (torch, TensorFlow, JAX) derive the backward pass for *any* architecture automatically — *automatic
differentiation*. You write the forward pass. The maths does not change.

## The same thing, in matrix form (Tutorial 7 Part B)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fw  <- forward(X, W1, b1, W2, b2); P <- fw$P; A1 <- fw$A1
dZ2 <- (P - y) / n                   # delta at the output          (n x 1)
dW2 <- t(A1) %*% dZ2                 # blame for hidden->output weights   (H x 1)
dA1 <- dZ2 %*% t(W2)                 # pass the blame back through W2     (n x H)
dZ1 <- dA1 * (1 - A1^2)              # through the tanh                   (n x H)
dW1 <- t(X) %*% dZ1                  # blame for input->hidden weights    (p x H)
W1 <- W1 - lr * dW1;  b1 <- b1 - lr * colSums(dZ1)
W2 <- W2 - lr * dW2;  b2 <- b2 - lr * sum(dZ2)
```
:::


Five lines of backpropagation, two of gradient descent. Run 500 times → the ring.

## Making training work

- **Initialisation**: small random weights, never all zero (identical units would get identical gradients and never
  differentiate). Xavier/Glorot (tanh) and He (ReLU) scale the randomness to the fan-in. Different seeds →
  slightly different networks; report it.
- **Vanishing / exploding gradients**: each backward step multiplies by a weight and an activation derivative;
  products of many small numbers → 0, of large ones → ∞. Fixes: ReLU, good init, **gradient clipping**,
  **batch normalisation**, **residual connections**.
- **Scale the inputs**: gradient descent on `hh_income` in ringgit and `age` in years spends all its steps on
  income. `step_normalize()` — not optional.

# 3 · Keeping it honest {.section-slide .center background-color="#0b2545" background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #0b2545 0%, #0f4c6e 55%, #13838f 100%)"}

## Networks overfit by default

1,411 weights on ~3,200 people per fold — about 2 people per parameter; a classical statistician wants 10–20
*events* per parameter. Left alone, training loss → 0, validation AUC falls, probabilities pile up at 0 and 1.

| Brake | Mechanism | parsnip / brulee |
|---|---|---|
| **weight decay (L2)** | add $\lambda\sum\theta^2$ to the loss → every step also shrinks the weights; the network's ridge regression | `penalty` |
| **dropout** | silence a random fraction of units on each training step; forces redundancy; ≈ an ensemble | `dropout` (brulee) |
| **early stopping** | stop when a validation slice stops improving | `stop_iter`, `validation` |
| smaller architecture | fewer units / layers | `hidden_units` |
| batch normalisation | stabilises, mildly regularises | brulee option |
| data augmentation | more (perturbed) examples | images, audio |

::: {.key}
Always early-stop when you can. Weight decay **or** dropout, not both (brulee). Tune width and decay together.
:::

## Architecture choices for tabular data

- **Width**: 8–64 units for a few thousand rows. **Depth**: one hidden layer is usually enough; two (32 → 16)
  occasionally helps; more rarely does.
- **Activation**: ReLU for depth; tanh/sigmoid fine for one small layer.
- **Output**: parsnip sets it from `set_mode()` — sigmoid/softmax/identity.
- **What to tune, in order**: learning rate (if not L-BFGS) → width → decay/dropout → epochs (early stopping) →
  batch size → depth.

**Universal approximation** says a wide-enough single layer *can* represent any continuous function. It does not
say gradient descent will *find* it, or that 3,200 people will *identify* it. Depth gets there with far fewer
parameters.

# 4 · In R {.section-slide .center background-color="#0b2545" background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #0b2545 0%, #0f4c6e 55%, #13838f 100%)"}

## The engines

| Engine | Layers | Backend | Install | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`nnet`** | 1 hidden | base R, BFGS | ships with R | today's hands-on; small tabular nets; always works |
| **`brulee`** | many | **torch** (libtorch, no Python) | `torch::install_torch()`, ~250 MB once | multi-layer MLPs inside tidymodels; dropout, early stopping, schedules |
| `torch` directly | anything | torch | as above | custom architectures, CNNs, RNNs in R |
| `keras3` | anything | TensorFlow / JAX / PyTorch via Python | Python env | largest ecosystem; most tutorials |
| `h2o` | MLP | Java | Java | big-data clusters |


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 0.01, epochs = 200) |> set_engine("nnet", MaxNWts = 10000) |> set_mode("classification")

mlp(hidden_units = c(32L, 16L), epochs = 150, learn_rate = 0.005, dropout = 0.2, penalty = 0, activation = "relu") |>
  set_engine("brulee", optimizer = "SGD", batch_size = 256, momentum = 0.9, stop_iter = 15, validation = 0.1) |>
  set_mode("classification")
```
:::


## `mlp()` arguments across engines

| parsnip | nnet | brulee | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hidden_units` | `size` (one layer) | integer or **vector** (one per layer) | width (and depth) |
| `penalty` | `decay` | `penalty` | weight decay (L2) |
| `epochs` | `maxit` | `epochs` | optimiser iterations / passes |
| `dropout` | — | `dropout` | fraction silenced per step |
| `activation` | sigmoid (fixed) | `"relu"`, `"elu"`, `"tanh"`, … | hidden non-linearity |
| `learn_rate` | — | `learn_rate` | step size |
| engine extras | `MaxNWts` (raise it!) | `optimizer`, `batch_size`, `momentum`, `stop_iter`, `validation`, `class_weights`, `rate_schedule` | |

## Tuning a network is tuning


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nn_tune_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, mlp(hidden_units = tune(), penalty = tune(), epochs = 200) |>
                         set_engine("nnet", MaxNWts = 10000) |> set_mode("classification"))
nn_params <- extract_parameter_set_dials(nn_tune_wf) |>
  update(hidden_units = hidden_units(range = c(2L, 24L)), penalty = penalty(range = c(-4, -0.5)))

nn_race <- tune_race_anova(nn_tune_wf, dm_folds, param_info = nn_params, grid = 16, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class))
nn_last <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(nn_tune_wf, select_best(nn_race, metric = "roc_auc")), dm_split)
```
:::


- Width and weight decay are the two that matter for one layer; learning rate and epochs join for deeper ones.
- Expect **more run-to-run variability** than trees (random initialisation). Repeated CV earns its keep.
- Explain it with `kernelshap()` (no TreeSHAP for a network) and this morning's `shapviz` plots. If network and trees agree
  on the structure, both are more believable.

# 5 · When not to use one {.section-slide .center background-color="#0b2545" background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #0b2545 0%, #0f4c6e 55%, #13838f 100%)"}

## The evidence on tabular data

| Study | Finding |
|---|---|
| Shwartz-Ziv & Armon 2022, *Information Fusion* | XGBoost beat the deep tabular models on the very datasets those models were published with |
| Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux 2022, NeurIPS | 45 datasets: tuned GBMs win on medium-sized tabular data; nets struggle with uninformative features and non-smooth targets |
| McElfresh et al. 2023, NeurIPS | 176 datasets: for most, the gap is smaller than the gain from tuning; nets win on some large, smooth problems |
| Christodoulou et al. 2019, *J Clin Epidemiol* | no benefit of ML over logistic regression across 71 clinical prediction studies, after bias |

::: {.key}
On a 5,000-row survey a well-regularised network **ties** boosted trees and logistic regression — and costs more
compute, more tuning, more variance and less interpretability. Tutorial 7 shows exactly that. It is a *finding*,
not a failure.
:::

## Where neural networks earn their keep

| Data | Architecture | Health examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Images** | CNNs, vision transformers | retinopathy, chest X-ray, pathology, dermatology, radiology triage |
| **Signals / waveforms** | 1-D CNN, RNN/LSTM, transformers | ECG, EEG, PPG, continuous monitoring |
| **Text** | transformers (BERT, GPT family) | clinical notes, coding, referral triage, literature |
| **Event sequences** | RNN, transformers | EHR trajectories, next-visit prediction |
| **Very large tabular** (10⁶+ rows) | MLP, TabNet, FT-Transformer | claims, national registries — sometimes |
| **Multimodal** | fused encoders | image + report + labs |

Common thread: inputs are **raw and high-dimensional**; the useful features (an edge, a QRS complex, a phrase) must
be *learned*. Tabular data arrives already feature-engineered — which is why trees do fine.

## Convolution, recurrence, attention — one slide each

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**CNN** — a 3×3 **filter** slides across the image and fires where it matches a pattern; layers of filters build
edges → textures → parts → objects; **pooling** shrinks and adds translation invariance. **Transfer learning**:
start from a net trained on millions of natural images, retrain the last layers on your 2,000 fundus photos.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**RNN / LSTM** — process a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state (memory); LSTM gates decide what to
keep and forget. ECG, vital-sign streams, early EHR-sequence models. Largely superseded by …
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Transformer** — every position looks at every other and learns *where to look* (**attention**); no recurrence,
massively parallel. The basis of BERT/GPT, modern vision models, and the medical foundation models now arriving.
:::
::::

## How deep learning fails in health

- **Shortcut learning**: pneumonia classifiers that read the portable-X-ray marker; skin-cancer models that detect the
  dermatologist's ruler; COVID CXR models that learned the hospital (DeGrave et al. 2021).
- **Dataset shift**: a new scanner, population or protocol — performance collapses silently.
- **Over-confidence**: badly calibrated out of the box (Guo et al. 2017) → temperature scaling / Platt before deployment.
- **Data and label hunger**; label noise propagates.
- **Reproducibility**: seeds, GPU non-determinism, undocumented pre-processing.
- **Equity**: under-performance on under-represented groups unless measured.

Same medicine as the rest of the workshop: leak-free splits **by patient**, honest resampling, calibration, subgroup
checks, explanations used as audits.
